title: The Man Who Would Be King
text:
Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan were two loafers and former soldiers in British India. They signed a contract with each other to give up drink and women and go to Kafiristan, a remote land in the mountains beyond Afghanistan, where they meant to make themselves kings. They set off with twenty rifles disguised as a mad priest and his servant.

In Kafiristan they trained villagers to shoot and won battle after battle. The people took Dravot for a god, the son of Alexander the Great. By a stroke of luck, Dravot recognized local rituals as resembling Freemasonry, and he used the signs of the lodge to take command of the priests. He became king, and Carnehan his general. Dravot began to dream of a great kingdom, an empire to hand to the Queen.

Then he decided that a king needed a queen, and he insisted on marrying a local girl, against Carnehan's warnings and the priests' fear. At the ceremony the terrified bride bit him, and blood ran down his beard. A god does not bleed. The people rose against them. Dravot was made to walk onto a rope bridge over a gorge, the ropes were cut, and he fell. Carnehan was crucified between two pine trees and survived.

Months later, a crippled, half mad Carnehan reached the narrator's newspaper office carrying Dravot's head in a bag, still wearing its gold crown. He died soon afterward.
lesson: Authority built on an illusion lasts only while you remember it is an illusion. The moment you start believing your own legend and ignoring your partners' warnings, it begins to fall.
people: Daniel Dravot, Peachey Carnehan, the narrator
location: British India (story set in Kafiristan, modern Afghanistan)
source: Rudyard Kipling, The Man Who Would Be King, 1888
